summary: Describes RPCSEC_GSS, a security flavor for ONC RPC that lets RPC-based protocols use the GSS-API for authentication and optional integrity or privacy protection. This makes it possible to plug different security mechanisms underneath RPC services such as NFS.

eli5.summary: It is a lock that fits onto a remote-call system, letting you choose from different kinds of keys to prove who you are and keep messages private.

questions: how does gss-api security work with rpc
what is the rpcsec_gss sequence window
subtitle: How ONC RPC services get authentication, integrity and privacy by plugging into the GSS-API.

tldr.problem: ONC RPC services needed stronger security than their existing flavors gave, and wanted to be independent of any one security mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: RPCSEC_GSS (flavor number 6) sets up a security context with GSS-API tokens, then protects each call with a header checksum and optionally integrity or privacy for the arguments and results, using a sequence-number window against replay.
tldr.outcome: RPC protocols can use any GSS-API mechanism, such as Kerberos V5, without changes to RPC itself. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5403.

today: RFC 2203 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5403. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Security Flavor Built on GSS-API
sections.content:
RFC 2203 defines the protocol of the RPCSEC_GSS security flavor for ONC RPC. Security flavors were historically called authentication flavors; this memo notes there are two other services besides authentication, namely integrity and privacy, and so defines a new flavor. It is described in XDR, and readers are assumed to know ONC RPC and the GSS-API framework.

The key idea is that RPCSEC_GSS uses GSS-API interfaces to provide security services independent of the underlying security mechanism. The flavor has been assigned the number 6, and two new auth_stat values are added: RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM (13) and RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM (14).
sections.eli5: RPC is a way for one computer to ask another to do a job. This adds a lock that works with many kinds of keys.

sections.title: Three Phases and the Credential
sections.content:
A session using RPCSEC_GSS has three phases: context creation, RPC data exchange and context destruction. Context creation and destruction use control messages that are not delivered to the service's procedures. They carry the service's program and version numbers and use procedure number NULLPROC (zero). A field in the credential, gss_proc, says whether a message is a control message or ordinary data.

The credential, rpc_gss_cred_t, holds four things for version 1: the control procedure (gss_proc), a sequence number (seq_num), the service requested (service) and a context handle. Version 0 is reserved for a possible future version negotiation protocol. The largest sequence number is MAXSEQ, 0x80000000.

There is no facility in the protocol to negotiate GSS-API mechanism identifiers or quality-of-protection (QOP) values. Implementations are expected to let the client specify them and the server enforce them per request, and an application may negotiate them in its own protocol or out of band. Any application protocol that references RPCSEC_GSS must list a mandatory set of { mechanism, QOP, service } triples. For example, a network filing protocol might require Kerberos V5 with the default QOP and the integrity service.
sections.eli5: Every conversation has three parts: agree on a secret, talk using the secret, and say goodbye. A little tag on each message says which part it is.

sections.title: Creating and Destroying a Context
sections.content:
The first request from the client creates a context. It uses NULLPROC, flavor RPCSEC_GSS and a gss_proc of RPCSEC_GSS_INIT; any further creation requests use RPCSEC_GSS_CONTINUE_INIT. The handle is empty in the first request and must equal the server's value afterwards. All creation requests carry a null verifier. The GSS-API token from GSS_Init_sec_context() rides in the call data, because RPC version 2 limits the credential and verifier bodies to 400 octets each, while GSS tokens can be longer than 800 octets.

The client must turn off replay_det_req_flag and sequence_req_flag in that call. RPC may run over unreliable transports, servers can be multi-threaded, and messages can arrive out of order, so RPCSEC_GSS provides its own replay protection that tolerates out-of-order delivery and dropped requests.

A successful reply carries rpc_gss_init_res: a handle, gss_major and gss_minor results of GSS_Accept_sec_context(), a seq_window and a gss_token. If gss_major is GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED, the client must send another creation request with the returned token. If it is GSS_S_COMPLETE, the data exchange phase starts with the next client request. Any other value means setup failed, and the handle and token are null. The context handle stays the same for the life of the context.

To end the session the client sends a control message with gss_proc set to RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY, procedure NULLPROC and no arguments, with a valid sequence number and header checksum. Both sides then destroy the context. If that request fails, the client need not do anything special, and servers should use an LRU or aging mechanism to clean up abandoned contexts.
sections.eli5: The two computers swap secret messages, maybe a few times, until both are sure who the other is. Then they get a membership number to use. At the end, the client hands it back.

sections.title: Protecting Data Requests and Replies
sections.content:
Once a context exists, each request uses gss_proc set to RPCSEC_GSS_DATA, the same version as at creation, the chosen service and the context handle. The seq_num may start at any value below MAXSEQ and must increase for each request. The verifier holds a checksum of the RPC header (up to and including the credential), computed with GSS_GetMIC() and the desired QOP. The QOP is implicit in the checksum, and the same QOP must be used for the data unless the service is rpc_gss_svc_none.

There are three levels of service, and the header format is the same for all of them:

  • None (rpc_gss_svc_none): arguments are sent as with AUTH_NONE. The header is still integrity protected, so the sender is still authenticated.
  • Integrity (rpc_gss_svc_integrity): the arguments, prefixed by the sequence number, are sent with a separate GSS_GetMIC() checksum.
  • Privacy (rpc_gss_svc_privacy): the same structure is encrypted with GSS_Wrap() with conf_req_flag TRUE.

For an accepted reply, the verifier is a checksum of the corresponding request's sequence number, with the same QOP. Results are formatted according to the same service as the request, in the same way the arguments were.
sections.eli5: You can send a postcard anyone can read, a postcard with a tamper-proof seal, or a locked box. Every envelope has a stamp proving who sent it.

sections.title: The Sequence Window
sections.content:
The server checks the version, the service, the context handle, the header checksum (with GSS_VerifyMIC()) and the sequence number. It keeps a window of seq_window sequence numbers ending at the highest one seen, N. If a higher number arrives and its header checksum verifies, the window slides forward. Numbers from N down to N - seq_window + 1 are acceptable, and the server remembers each one it has seen with a bit. A number below the window, or a repeat inside it, is silently discarded.

Silent discard is deliberate: the server cannot tell whether a duplicate came from the client, the network, routing quirks or a replay attack, and dropping it lets a client recover after a timeout. The client must increment the sequence number even when retrying a request with the same transaction identifier. The server picks seq_window based on how many requests it expects to process simultaneously, for example the number of server threads. The RFC says there are no known security issues with a large window, and the main cost is the space for tracking.

For integrity and privacy the server also checks that the QOP matches the header's, and it rejects the request with GARBAGE_ARGS if the sequence number inside the body differs from the one in the credential.
sections.eli5: It is like a ticket checker who remembers the last few ticket numbers. A ticket used twice or too old is quietly ignored, so a copied ticket does not work.

sections.title: Errors and Context Refresh
sections.content:
A denied data request may use the two new auth_stat values. RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM is returned when the server has no context for the handle (for example it was destroyed early on an LRU basis, or the server rebooted), or when the header checksum fails to verify. RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM is returned when the sequence number exceeds the maximum, or when credentials go stale, as with Kerberos V5 ticket expiry. In both cases the client must refresh the context and retry. For other errors the client must not refresh until the problem is fixed. A mismatched version or a bad credential gives AUTH_BADCRED. Neither new value can be returned for context creation requests.

The RFC also maps GSS-API failures to responses:

  • Failure to generate the reply verifier with GSS_GetMIC() gives a denied reply with RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM.
  • Failure to verify the request verifier gives a denied reply with RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM.
  • Failure to verify or unwrap the call arguments gives an accepted reply with status GARBAGE_ARGS.
  • Failure to sign or wrap the results sends no response; the failure goes to the server application, which can log it.
sections.eli5: If the club loses your membership card, you are told to sign up again and retry. If you just did something wrong, signing up again will not help.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With the privacy service, only the call arguments and results are encrypted. The RPC program, version and procedure numbers travel in the clear, because encrypting them would have required changing the RPC header. The RFC argues an attacker can often learn program and version numbers anyway by querying rpcbind, and that RPCSEC_GSS still improves on prior RPC security. Designers worried about this may add a sub-procedure field inside the service arguments.

An attacker cannot push the server's sequence number up without a request that passes the header checksum, but if verifying the checksum is expensive, bogus requests with far-above-window numbers could waste processing resources. Requests within or below the window are silently discarded, so a server may skip checksum verification for them. The protocol does not address attacks that block or steal messages without detection, as protecting against that would amount to assuming state in the RPC service, and RPCSEC_GSS does not make it worse.
sections.eli5: The message inside is locked, but the label on the outside shows which office it goes to. That is a known trade-off.
